Schedule 1-hour dedicated throughput run with Sofia and Derek to validate 99th percentile latency on p40s (Derek) - due 2026-05-14

action_items: Derek Alvarez: run 24h synthetic workload with customer prompt mix and share CSV of latency percentiles - due 2026-05-14

header:
Date: 2026-05-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (BlueOrbit VP Eng), Sofia Martinez (BlueOrbit Dir MLOps), Raj Patel (BlueOrbit Finance), Hannah Li (BlueOrbit Product), Ethan Brooks (BlueOrbit SRE)
summary: Quarterly business review focusing on cost-to-serve, recent reliability incidents, and alignment on roadmap priorities. Agreement to run an engineering throughput validation and to iterate pricing scenarios; customer requested additional SOC2/network artifacts for procurement and flagged need for stronger 99th percentile latency guarantees on long-chat endpoints.
topics: uptime and latency SLOs especially 99th pct
roadmap items: private VPC control plane, dedicated pools, caching suggestions
questions: What would dedicated capacity look like at our 95% utilization?
How does KV cache/ prefix cache work across long chat sessions?
Can you guarantee data residency for EU-only traffic?
transcript_body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: OK, welcome everyone, thanks for making time for the QBR, um, we'll run through usage, costs, the recent outage, and then roadmap priorities. I think we have about 50 minutes, so let's try to keep pacing.

[00:18] Liam O'Connor: Thanks Maya. I'll hand it off to Sofia to start with consumption and the SRE context.

[00:25] Sofia Martinez: Yeah thanks. Quick tl;dr: tokens are up about 22% q/q mainly from the new chat feature. Most volume is from two endpoints — conversation-hub and answer-stream. We also had the incident on 4/18 where a model fallback loop caused elevated latencies, that impacted about 1.5% of sessions but we saw 99th spike to ~6s.

[00:52] Derek Alvarez: Got it. For context, that fallback loop — was it a routing policy that retried to a higher-capacity model or was it multiple route hops?

[00:59] Sofia Martinez: It looks like the route policy bounced between region fallback and model fallback. The customer set a "prefer-cheap" policy that cascaded. So it tried small quantized variant, failed, then retried to the full model and then congested.

[01:12] Ethan Brooks: Right, from our side the burst bumped the queueing, and our observation is that the KV cache didn't warm because the requests were slightly shifted by session id. So cache hit rate dropped.

[01:27] Priya Nair: On our side we've flagged that as an opportunity — Redwood has automatic cache hints and also model variant fallback rules, we can show how to prevent the back-and-forth. Derek will walk through options later.

[01:40] Raj Patel: Quick finance question before we go deeper: that kind of replays — does it double bill tokens when retries happen? We need to show that in our forecasting.

[01:48] Maya Chen: Good call. Billing only counts committed tokens. Retries that produce additional tokens are billed; however we can reduce retries with smarter fallback policies and prefix caching so you don't re-render the same tokens. We'll include cost impact scenarios in the pricing doc.

[02:03] Hannah Li: Can you clarify "prefix caching"? We heard about KV cash earlier in the notes — is that the same?

[02:10] Derek Alvarez: Yes, prefix caching and KV cache are related. KV cache stores transformer activations for continuation, prefix caching stores tokens/partial outputs for repeated prompts — it's not perfect for every use case but for chat where prompts have common prefixes it's high ROI.

[02:27] Liam O'Connor: Cool, what timeline to get a run that demonstrates 99th percentile improvements? Our SLA for product is pretty strict.

[02:35] Derek Alvarez: We can set up a controlled run — need the exact prompt distribution and session characteristics. If Sofia can send the daily token histogram and list of top endpoints, I can spin a 24 hour synthetic with your concurrency and share P50/P95/P99.

[02:49] Sofia Martinez: I'll share that by Monday.

[02:52] Maya Chen: Great. Ok moving to cost: Raj, any specific asks beyond visibility?

[03:00] Raj Patel: Mostly visibility and options. Right now the hosted invoice average unit cost per 1k tokens is fine for dev, but production peaks are killing margins. We were evaluating Dedicated as a path to predictable unit economics — want to see a hosted vs dedicated vs hybrid comparison with break-evens.

[03:16] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll produce three scenarios: current hosted baseline, a reserved dedicated pool at a 6–12 month commit, and a hybrid where heavy real-time routes go to dedicated and background batch to hosted. Derek will model expected throughput and Priya will model the SLA/contract differences.

[03:32] Raj Patel: And include quantization options — are there recommended quantization profiles that maintain accuracy for our NLU tasks?

[03:38] Derek Alvarez: Yes, we did a QoR sweep last quarter on a similar workload. Some 8-bit quant profiles preserve top-level intent accuracy, but for fine-grained entity extraction you may need fp16 or Q4_0. We'll include per-model guidance.

[03:50] Hannah Li: Any immediate quick wins? We have a backlog of small changes but limited engineering cycles.

[03:56] Priya Nair: Short list: 1) route heavy "system prompts" to cached variants, 2) reduce retry window, 3) enable early prefix-caching for chat for common opening lines. Those three typically buy 10–30% cost reduction with minimal engineering lift.

[04:17] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. On reliability — the outage RCA, what's the follow-up? Is there an action plan to stop policy cascades?

[04:26] Derek Alvarez: Yes — immediate config change is to add a circuit-breaker on cross-model retries and limit the depth of fallback cascades. Longer term, we recommend a canary rollout for any routing policy changes and a trace sampling policy to catch cascading failures early.

[04:41] Ethan Brooks: For canaries, do you support sticky session routing to same instance pool so warm KV cache persists across retries?

[04:50] Derek Alvarez: We do. You can enable sticky routing for session affinity, which improves cache warmness at the cost of slight load balancing constraints. It's usually worth it for low-latency chat flows.

[05:04] Sofia Martinez: One regulatory ask — EU data residency. Can Redwood guarantee traffic only touches EU regions and provide a EU-only control plane?

[05:12] Maya Chen: We have a Private option with EU-only control plane and VPC connectors; for hosted we can pin region routing to EU+, but if you need legal guarantees we should look at Private deployment or Dedicated in EU. We'll attach the network diagram and SOC2 docs.

[05:28] Raj Patel: Please send the SOC2. Procurement needs that for the renewal packet.

[05:33] Priya Nair: Will add SOC2 attestation and network diagram to the shared drive after the call.

[05:38] Maya Chen: Great. Now roadmap items — we wanted to call out a couple of things: private VPC control plane GA (Q3), improved per-route billing granularity (Q2), and a caching UI in Console to visualize prefix cache hits (Q3). Any questions on those?

[05:54] Hannah Li: Per-route billing granularity in Q2 would help our chargeback model. Can we get an ETA on console export?

[06:02] Priya Nair: The early export API will be available next week in beta; production UI export slated for June. We'll give you access to the beta.

[06:11] Liam O'Connor: On private control plane — what's the difference between Dedicated and Private? We might confuse terms.

[06:18] Maya Chen: Good question. Dedicated is reserved capacity on Redwood-managed infra (predictable throughput). Private is customer-managed network options with a private control plane, e.g., VPC peering or on-prem connector for sensitive data. Both can be in EU regions. Dedicated is about capacity; Private is about network and compliance.

[06:34] Raj Patel: For procurement, do we get an enterprise addendum for Data Processing Agreement?

[06:38] Priya Nair: Yes, enterprise customers get a DPA and can add clauses for residency and retention; we'll route that through Legal and copy you.

[06:45] Derek Alvarez: Back to engineering: Sofia, when you send the token histogram, also include seq length distribution so we can tune batching and kernel selection. It's surprising how much P99 improves when you match real sequence-length distributions.

[06:58] Sofia Martinez: Sequence lengths are variable; many sessions are 1k+ tokens. We'll export the distribution.

[07:05] Maya Chen: Great. Quick pricing note — our AE will include a 10% credit for the pilot and a mapping of break-even points for dedicated for three traffic scenarios.

[07:16] Raj Patel: On renewal — renewal date is 2026-07-15. We'd like contractual SLA around 99.9% on critical endpoints. Is that doable with dedicated?

[07:25] Maya Chen: Dedicated can get you closer to deterministic throughput and SLA-backed latency targets; we can discuss a 99.9% uptime commitment on dedicated with an SLA addendum and service credits. We'll confirm exact terms with Sales/Legal.

[07:37] Liam O'Connor: One more operational item — our security team wants proof of key management, do you integrate with our KMS?

[07:44] Priya Nair: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. For hosted we can provide envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key integrations in certain tiers. We'll send the integration guide.

[07:58] Hannah Li: If we move some heavy endpoints to dedicated, how long to provision a dedicated pool? We're planning a summer launch.

[08:05] Maya Chen: For standard SKUs it's 2–4 weeks once there's a signed commit and infra seats; for larger custom clusters it could be longer. We'll provide a timeline tied to the commit.

[08:18] Derek Alvarez: Also note that once dedicated is provisioned you may need a short warm-up period to populate KV caches; we can script a warm-up workflow to mitigate cold-starts.

[08:29] Sofia Martinez: Good to know. Ok, any blockers from our side to start the pilot? We have budget hold but can shift if procurement sees the SOC2 and the pricing scenarios look reasonable.

[08:41] Raj Patel: Procurement needs the security pack and the three-scenario pricing, then we'll run procurement.

[08:48] Maya Chen: We will send both. Priya will own the SOC2 packet; Maya will send pricing; Derek will schedule throughput run.

[08:58] Liam O'Connor: For the throughput run, include a mix of long-chat sessions and short queries. Our production mix is about 30% long chats.

[09:07] Derek Alvarez: Noted. We'll mirror that mix.

[09:12] Maya Chen: Any other questions?

[09:15] Ethan Brooks: One final ask — can you share a simple checklist for optimizing prompts for cost? Our product writers sometimes create very long system messages.

[09:23] Derek Alvarez: Yes, we have a 1-pager with best practices: trimming system prompts, moving static context to prefix cache, using structured outputs where possible to reduce token churn. We'll attach that.

[09:36] Priya Nair: OK, 1 minute wrap. So to recap: Maya sends pricing scenarios and pilot credit, Priya sends SOC2 and network diagram, Derek runs 24h synthetic throughput with Sofia's token distro, Sofia sends histograms and top endpoints, Raj will engage procurement once materials are in. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the throughput validation.

[09:56] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, appreciate the collaboration. We'll get those artifacts over by Friday.

[10:02] Liam O'Connor: Thanks team, bye.

[10:05] (meeting ends)
